episodes.183267: Increased moisture behind a backdoor front across eastern New Mexico led to the development of scattered storms across the east slopes of the central mountain chain growing upscale as they moved east. Some of the storms briefly became severe, producing strong wind gusts at Tucumcari, Roswell, and near Bitter Lake Wildlife Refuge.
episodes.183286: Severe thunderstorms were observed across parts of southeast Wyoming the evening of 9 September 2023. Very large hail was reported across Converse, Platte and Goshen Counties during this time.
episodes.183441: A couple of showers and thunderstorms developed along the sea breeze the afternoon of September 10th. The southern most storm moved southwest through eastern Hidalgo County and produced sporadic straight-line wind damage near Mile 13 Road and FM493. Damage included a metal barn blown across the road and crumpled up 20 to 30 yards into the field across the street, a large tree down, and some awning damage to The End of the Trail Sports Bar #1.
episodes.183574: A hot and muggy airmass was conducive to heavy downpours over eastern Massachusetts and Rhode Island when a de-amplifying shortwave moved across the region. It also had support from a moderately strong jet aloft and plenty of moisture. Weak boundary layer winds made for slow moving storms which contributed to flooding.
episodes.183575: A hot and muggy airmass was conducive to heavy downpours over eastern Massachusetts and Rhode Island when a de-amplifying shortwave moved across the region. It also had support from a moderately strong jet aloft and plenty of moisture. Weak boundary layer winds made for slow moving storms which contributed to flooding.
episodes.183610: A thunderstorm briefly became severe over far eastern Custer County, producing a few wind gusts of around 60 mph.
episodes.183611: A thunderstorm became severe over western portions of Crook County, producing quarter sized hail in the Pine Haven area.
episodes.183622: An isolated instance of flash flooding occurred due to heavy rain associated with showers and thunderstorms.
episodes.183738: An isolated severe thunderstorm produced localized wind damage east of Fredericksburg, Virginia.
episodes.183756: A cold front which moved south of the region early on the ninth led to easterly upslope flow across much of the West Texas region into eastern New Mexico during the afternoon. Thunderstorms were able to form on the higher terrain of eastern New Mexico and move into the South Plains during the evening hours. A strong outflow boundary developed well out ahead of the line of thunderstorms producing a severe wind gust at the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Sundown (Cochran County). One severe thunderstorm severe wind gust occurred near Friona (Parmer County).
episodes.183910: An upper level system brought numerous slow moving thunderstorms to East Tennessee, producing a couple of reports of damaging winds and one of flash flooding.
episodes.184026: Thunderstorms produced locally heavy rain in extreme southeastern Pennsylvania on the evening of September 10.  Rainfall totals were as high as 2 to 3 inches.
episodes.184351: As hurricane Lee moved well north of the region, external feeding bands from the hurricane reached the local islands. Additionally, the moisture advected into the region, contributed to the development of strong showers along the Cordillera Central and southern Puerto Rico. A few flooding reports, and even a funnel cloud was detected within this activity.
episodes.184447: Unsettled weather was on the docket each afternoon from September 9th through the 12th across West Virginia as a result of a stationary frontal boundary residing over the area. While severe parameters were not impressive during this time frame, afternoon thunderstorms had enough gumption to promote isolated tree and power line damage across parts of the state. High moisture levels festering over these several days also resulted in high water issues along local roads, especially in Raleigh County, where flood prone areas in the Beckley area took on a decent amount of street flooding on September 10th. Convection was primarily diurnally driven during this time, so the severe and flash flooding concerns quickly tapered down after sunset each day.
episodes.184591: Diurnally enhanced showers and storms moving west to east encountered the inland progressing east coast sea breeze during the afternoon. Locally strong thunderstorms developed near boundary mergers.
episodes.184759: An influx of moisture restarted a brief active period moving towards the middle of September. As a result, the region saw a couple of days with scattered showers and thunderstorms, some of which produced strong gusty winds, with one producing a landspout.
episodes.184892: A cold front moved across central Wyoming and brought large hail to portions of Natrona and Fremont Counties. There were numerous reports of hail from penny to golf ball size across the two aforementioned counties. With the slow movement of the storms, hail accumulated several inches in some places. The two hardest hit areas were along Highway 259 and Interstate 25 south of Midwest in Natrona County as well as Highway 28 over South Pass. Plows had to clear the hail of the road at South Pass.
episodes.184924: A strong thunderstorm produced heavy rainfall over the City of Galax, VA at rates of 3 to 4 inches per hour.  Multiple personal weather stations just north of the downtown observed about 2 inches of rainfall as a storm total amount, with the one inch falling during the first 20 minutes of the storm.
episodes.185572: A warm front moved eastward towards the Kentucky border counties during the day on September 9th, 2023. It then stalled during the afternoon and evening along the highest terrain just east of the state. Showers and thunderstorms developed just ahead of this front and moved westward into eastern Kentucky. As the front stalled, the storms began back-building and training across some of the same areas. Bell County was the hardest hit in eastern Kentucky, receiving over 3.5 inches in a 2 hour time period. Multiple instances of flash flooding were reported as a result.
episodes.185586: A good bit of moisture worked its way into the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles on the 9th through the 11th. The upper level pattern favored upper level help for storms to travel into the combined Panhandles from the west and northwest during the late afternoon into overnight hours. The first night on the 9th a couple of strong supercell thunderstorms dropped hail up to 2.5 in diameter in the western Oklahoma Panhandle. More widespread storms managed to drop hail up to 1.5, but these storms also produced several severe wind gusts upwards of 80 plus mph on the night of the 10th across much of the combined Panhandles.
episodes.185587: A good bit of moisture worked its way into the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles on the 9th through the 11th. The upper level pattern favored upper level help for storms to travel into the combined Panhandles from the west and northwest during the late afternoon into overnight hours. The first night on the 9th a couple of strong supercell thunderstorms dropped hail up to 2.5 in diameter in the western Oklahoma Panhandle. More widespread storms managed to drop hail up to 1.5, but these storms also produced several severe wind gusts upwards of 80 plus mph on the night of the 10th across much of the combined Panhandles.
episodes.185647: Scattered thunderstorms developed along a stationary front which was located over the central Sandhills, around 1 PM CDT on September 9th. This activity quickly became severe and tracked to the southeast into Custer County. Additional thunderstorm activity developed over Logan County and northern Lincoln County and tracked south into eastern Hayes and Frontier Counties through the early evening hours. Several hail reports, up to two inches in diameter and wind gusts up to 70 MPH occurred.
episodes.185759: A frontal boundary and low pressure system located to the west and east of eastern New York was the focus for rounds of showers and thunderstorms each day September 7-9. Strong to severe thunderstorms were more widespread on September 7-8. These storms resulted in numerous reports of tree and powerline damage, as well as thousands without power and several road closures. Some school districts across Columbia County delayed classes or closed on September 8 as a result of the severe thunderstorms on September 7.
episodes.185774: During the afternoon hours, an isolated thunderstorm developed over Cheyenne County, Kansas and moved southeast across the area. More scattered storms developed over portions of extreme Southwest Nebraska and East-Central Colorado, moving south-southeast through the evening hours. These storms produced large hail up to the size of limes and thunderstorm wind gusts of 58 to 77 mph. The largest hail was reported in Wheeler while the strongest wind gusts were observed in Gove County where three semi trucks were also rolled over.
episodes.185785: During the late afternoon to evening hours, scattered thunderstorms developed over extreme Southwest Nebraska. These storms produced thunderstorm wind gusts of 58 to 61 mph with the strongest gusts occurring near the town of Trenton, Nebraska.
episodes.185786: During the afternoon hours, an isolated supercell thunderstorm developed and produced pea to quarter sized hail over the town of Lydia in southern Wichita County, Kansas.
episodes.185795: Isolated severe thunderstorms in advance of a frontal boundary produced damaging winds across portions of the Middle Peninsula.
episodes.185796: Scattered thunderstorms in advance of a frontal boundary produced heavy rain which caused flash flooding across portions of eastern Virginia.
episodes.185805: Thunderstorms developed along a frontal boundary in Central Texas and moved southward into South Central Texas. Some of these storms produced large hail and severe wind gusts.
episodes.185833: Thunderstorms brought hail and wind to portions of western Kansas.
episodes.185874: A stationary front remained over the Mid Atlantic region and led to multiple rounds of thunderstorms. While wind shear was weak, instability was high creating a favorable environment for localized damaging winds during the late morning and afternoon hours.
episodes.185877: A stationary frontal system over northeastern Pennsylvania combined with a weak upper level disturbance to focus heavy rain producing thunderstorms over the area. Torrential downpours over just a couple of hours accumulated between 3 to 5 inches of rainfall in small stream basins above the large metropolitan area known as the Lackawanna-Wyoming Valley. Severe flash flooding resulted in many road and bridge washouts around the local region. Motorists were stranded on urban streets and the flooding resulted in the deaths of two people who attempted to evacuate their vehicle into rushing waters. Another four people were seriously injured when their vehicle crashed into the remnants of a washed out bridge. The perpetual thunderstorms and flooding also shut down the Luzerne County Fair. Overall damages to the region as a result of this severe flooding are estimated at around 20 million dollars.
episodes.185986: A broad upper-level disturbance initiated scattered shower and thunderstorms across North and North-Central GA during the early afternoon hours. Minor instability meant a few thunderstorms became strong to severe. Storms were slow moving and reached the eastern portion of the CWA late in the evening. Late storm consolidation led to isolated severe wind and flooding.
episodes.186145: Isolated showers and thunderstorms developed each afternoon during the weekend of 9-10 September, mainly over areas south of US-50. Subtropical moisture steadily flowing north along the western periphery of a longwave ridge centered over the US/Mexico border moistened mid-levels across southern portions of our CWA increased storm chances to 20-30%. Hazards included stronger outflow winds, frequent lightning, localized areas of heavy rainfall, and the increased chance for small hail in stronger storm cores.
episodes.186175: Isolated to scattered thunderstorms developed in the vicinity of a stationary front across portions of southeast South Carolina from the afternoon into the early evening hours. The thunderstorms produced strong, gusty winds and cloud-to-ground lightning strikes.
episodes.186247: Scattered slow-moving thunderstorms developed across the North Carolina Piedmont during the afternoon and evening. One evening storm cluster became nearly stationary across Union County, resulting very heavy rainfall and flash flooding.

events.narrative: The US-189 at Deer Creek Dam mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 59 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

The Carbon County Regional Airport/Buck Davis Field ASOS recorded a period of wind gusts to 61 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.
A few trees near Arthur were blown down by powerful thunderstorm winds.
In Big Isaac, Laurel Run rose out of its banks and inundated the intersection of Big Isaac Road and Independence Road with three to four feet of water.
Social media reports flash flooding along U.S. Route 11 near the gas station with multiple occupied vehicles stranded with water to the bumpers.

Leggetts Creek flooding from South Abington Township to the Lackawanna River in Scranton. Severe flooding of residental structures on Leggett Street, Gilbert Street and Rockwell Street is occurring with evacuations underway.
Eight Mile Draw station.
Flooding along both Colwyn and Pennlyn Avenues near Cumberland Gap.
Mesonet station reported a 61 mph gust at the location.
A 58 mph thunderstorm wind gust was reported via ASOS station KMCK at the McCook Airport.
Cannon Air Force Base.
Little Bull Run flooded onto Artemus Road. Road was closed.
Toby Creek is well out of its banks, flooding an unknown number of homes and businesses.
Bridges washed out in Falls Township along Oak Drive, Dickinson Road and Deerfield Drive. Residents cut off from homes and evacuation routes.
A mesonet station (DEXC1-Dexter) located 13.0 mi ENE Crestview, CA, reported a storm total rainfall amount of 0.74 inches.
Pea to nickel sized hail reported over a duration of twenty-one minutes.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts measured at 55 kts by the Bird RAWS site at the Lyndon B. Johnson National Historical Park.
Nickel to quarter sized hail reported covering Interstate 25 near the Platte and Converse County line. A nearby WYDOT sensor reported zero visibility with heavy rain and wind gusts to 51 mph.

Several sources reported flash flooding developed across northwest Union County after 3 to 5 inches of rain fell in just a couple of hours from a nearly stalled thunderstorm cluster. Chinkapin Creek overflowed its banks in the Unionville area. Multiple roads were inundated in the Wesley Chapel area due to stream flooding as well as poor drainage. Several vehicles were stalled in flood water. Three people had to be rescued when water from a flooding stream surrounded their homes along Goldmine Rd in Wesley Chapel.
Tree down 2100 Block Hwy 59 .
Report of up to quarter sized hail.
Report received via social media of half dollar sized hail at location. Possibly larger size as hail was not collected and measured immediately.
Tree and powerlines down at Hwy 98 and Hwy 441.
There was a house on fire due to a lightning strike.
A trained spotter reported golf ball sized hail 4 miles N of Fort Laramie.
The public reported ping-pong ball sized hail 2 miles S of Douglas. Received via mPING.
Half dollar sized hail reported 4 miles WSW of Douglas. Minor roof damage reported.
Golf ball sized hail was reported in Douglas.
A 59 mph wind gust was measured by a mesonet over the span of two minutes.
Kansas Highway Patrol reported three semi trucks rolled over due to thunderstorm wind gusts estimated to be 70 mph. The semi trucks were blown over between mile markers 99 and 104 on I-70.
A trained spotter reported 2-inch diameter hail 1 mile N of Fort Laramie.
Mesonet station KKSPARK1 reported a 62 mph wind gust at the location.
The public reported half dollar sized hail 4 miles W of Douglas. Received via mPING.
A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Friona measured a wind gust of 58 mph.
A trained spotter reported golf ball sized hail at mile marker 34 on Highway 26 between Fort Laramie and Lingle.
Mesonet station KKSQUINT10 reported a thunderstorm wind gust of 58 mph.
Water was flowing over State Route 9 near Academy Street in Poughkeepsie.
Reported via mesonet station OVEK1.
A trained spotter reported half dollar sized hail 1 mile W of Lingle. Mostly hail, very little rain.

A single car crash occurred at this location as a result of the rural water crossing being compromised by flash flooding. The bridge gave way beneath the moving vehicle which then crashed into the remnants of the culvert/bridge system. All four occupants of the vehicle were severely injured and rushed to nearby hospitals.
A storm chaser measured 2.8-inch diameter hail 5 miles ESE of Fort Laramie.
A thunderstorm produced nickel size hail in St. Hedwig.
Mesonet station KKSUTICA3 reported a 70 mph thunderstorm wind gust.
A trained spotter found 1-inch hail on the ground accumulated several inches deep, approximately 4 miles W of Guernsey. Estimated time hail fell based on radar.

Thunderstorm winds caused damage at a local marina, lifting the roof off of a boat house and dropping it on several nearby boats. After a review of the radar data, photographs of the damage, and in consultation with the local Emergency Manager, the National Weather Service concluded that the damage that occurred was caused by straight line winds.
An Emergency Manager reported roads covered in hail accumulation 2 miles NW of Veteran. Largest hail stone was golf ball size.
Kansas State mesonet site reported the 75 wind gust at 10m.
An Emergency Manager reported quarter sized hail in Yoder.
A trained spotter reported hail accumulating to several inches deep 1 mile ESE of Yoder. Largest stone was ping-pong ball size.
Broadcast media relay of measured wind gust report at main street and Santa Fe Street in South Garden City.
Lightning struck a tree on Dogwood Circle and caused it to catch fire.

The City of Galax 911 Center reported that Main Street (VA Highway 89) was briefly flooded in the downtown area due to poor drainage caused by a clogged storm sewer.  One vehicle was stranded in the flood waters until the flooding receded.  No damage was reported.
In Cranston, Scituate Ave was flooded.
In Wayland, Bridge Rd and Anthony Rd were flooded.
In Cohasset, a portion of Chief Justice Cushing Rd was flooded and impassable.
In Providence, there was water covering Rt 10 at Union Ave.

High water was observed in several neighborhoods in Beckley. These included the intersections of Cannaday Street and Koch Avenue, Pice Street and Vance Drive, Hedrick Street and Little Street, and Bibb Avenue and Hartley Avenue. High water was also observed spilling into the yard of a home along Klaus Street.
In Rockland, portion of Rt 53 was flooded with water up to car windows.

events.narrative: The NOS station FRDF1 Fernandina Beach measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 49 mph.
In Providence, multiple water rescues were done for vehicles stranded in flood waters. Rt 10 was closed and several manhole covers were pushed up.
In Acton, Rt 27 was closed by Kelly Corner.
In Tewksbury, Mt Pleasant St underpass was flooded.

Bluffton Fire Department reported that lightning struck a home on Pine View Drive as well as a nearby tree. The lightning strike started a fire in the attic of the home and produced significant damage.
A retired National Weather Service meteorologist reported ping pong ball size hail along Arapahoe Roach Road to the north of Pavillion.

There were numerous reports of quarter to golf ball size hail the south and southwest of Midwest from Interstate 25 to Wyoming Highway 259. The hail accumulated a few inches along Highway 259, leading to travel being hampered for a few hours.
A few one inch hailstones were reported. Hail fell over the location approximately three minutes.
Several reports from the general public indicated a funnel cloud, observed from Salinas Speedway toward the mountains.
Flash flooding was reported on Hudgins Farm Road. Water was about one foot deep.
Rainfall total of 2.00 inches was reported in 50 minutes, and 2.97 inches of rain was reported in 2 hours 30 minutes.
Pictures from social media shows a metal structure crumpled up and blown several yards into the field across the street. Timing estimated by radar.
Pictures from social media show awning/roof damage to The End of the Trail Sports Bar #1 along FM493.
Pictures from social media show a large tree down in the backyard of a house across the street from Rick & Ron's Auto Sales. Minor roof damage was noted by the owner.
A thunderstorm moved southeastward and brought local severe hail. Hail from penny to occasionally quarter size was reported from near Bar Nunn to southeast of Evansville.
Philmont Avenue was closed due to flooding at Tomlinson Road in Lower Moreland Township.
Roadway flooding with some roads becoming impassable in the Parkwood and Normandy sections of Northeast Philadelphia.
Minor flooding occurred along the Pennypack Creek in Northeast Philadelphia.

Trained spotters and a National Weather Service employee reported hail from dime to 1.33 inch-sized from near Sinks Canyon State Park to South Pass. The hail accumulated several inches near Red Canyon along Highway 28, and snow plows had to be called out to clear the hail off the road.
